catalog_quote: Stress is not thoroughly researched. It is located on the first high toned syllable. In words with only low tones it is located on the first syllable (Reh 1985, 78).In words with affixes the location of stress is determined by:1. Tones in the affixes2. Tones in the root3. Number of syllables in the root4. Vowel length in the first syllable of the root If the root is monosyllabic, or contains only low tones and a short vowel in the first syllable or has the sequence LH.There are some lexical oppositions.If the word is sufficiently long, high toned prefixes may get a secondary stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given. After Stevenson, stress is said to matter more than tone in the Kadugli-Krongo languages; stress is 'sometimes linked with tone', and the two Krongo examples ‘korugut 'husks' (initial stress) vs ku'rigt 'kidneys' (second-syllable stress) show stress on different syllables in words of similar shape, i.e. stress position is lexically variable rather than fixed. A stressed vowel may be followed by consonant length (p. 301: consonant length 'also occurs in emphatic speech, or after a stressed vowel'; 'indummo, Pl. nugu-ndu'ma-ne ostrich'). Final vowels are described as unstressed and often semi-mute in Krongo (p. 300), which is consistent with non-final stress but is not stated as a rule. Tone and stress are not marked in the rest of the chapter.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Dialect note: final semi-mute (unstressed) vowels are 'lacking' in the Western dialects of the group. The tone-doublet examples in 2a are unlabelled ('in some languages'); only the 2b stress examples are explicitly KRONGO.
new_statements.identity_note: Chapter 19 treats the Kadugli-Krongo group as a unit (Kamdang, Keiga, Miri, Kadugli, Katcha, Krongo; Western vs Eastern dialects). The stress examples in sec. 2b are explicitly labelled KRONGO and the unstressed-final-vowel remark says 'especially in KRONGO'; the tone doublets in 2a are unlabelled ('in some languages'). Data are second-hand from R. C. Stevenson's 1956-57 Nuba Mountains survey plus personal communication.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for where Krongo word stress falls is stated. After Stevenson, T&B report for the Kadugli-Krongo group that tone matters less than stress but lexical tone doublets exist in some languages (nyá 'hill' / nyà 'wind'; ofó 'to vomit' / 'ôfò 'mound'); for KRONGO specifically that stress is 'sometimes linked with tone', shown by the doublet 'kûrùgù 'husks' (initial stress, circumflex on the first vowel) vs ku'rûgù 'kidneys' (second-syllable stress, circumflex on the second vowel), i.e. stress sits on the syllable with the marked (high/falling) tone; that stress is connected with consonant length ('ndummo, Pl. nugu-ndu'ma-nɛ 'ostrich'; long consonants also 'after a stressed vowel'); that final unstressed vowels are often semi-mute in Krongo (isi 'fire'); and that tone and stress are not marked in the rest of the chapter. Coded tone language with a stress statement: tone present, stress discussed and tied to tone, no placement algorithm.
new_statements.exceptions: None as rules; only 'sometimes linked with tone', consonant length after a stressed vowel, and semi-mute final unstressed vowels (absent in the Western dialects of the group).
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's ch. 19 treats the Kadugli-Krongo (Kadu) group as a whole from Stevenson's Nuba Mountains survey (Kadugli, Katcha, Miri, Keiga, Kamdang, Tulishi, Krongo etc.); the two stress examples are explicitly flagged KRONGO (Krongo proper of the Krongo hills), while the tonal doublets are attributed only to 'some languages' of the group and the semi-mute final vowels to Krongo especially. The catalog's primary source, Reh 1985, describes Krongo of Tabanya (Nìinò mó-dì).

readall_conflicts: No placement conflict. Tucker & Bryan 1966:301 (after Stevenson 1956-57) state no rule for Krongo stress placement; they say stress is 'sometimes linked with tone' and illustrate initial vs second-syllable stress (‘korugut 'husks' / ku'rigt 'kidneys'), which is compatible with the catalog record (Reh 1985:78 via StressTyp2: stress on the first high-toned syllable, else initial, with morphological/tonal/length interactions and some lexical oppositions). Two points of tension in emphasis only: (i) Stevenson ranks stress above tone for the Kadugli-Krongo group ('tone is less important than stress'), whereas Reh describes Krongo as a H/L tone language whose stress follows the tones; (ii) the statement already held by the project from this same T&B passage is labelled 'lexical (unpredictable)', a label that rests only on the two example words and that I would replace by 'tone language with a stress statement' (same text, different label). Separately, the DOI on record for this work (10.4324/9781315105192-20) belongs to the reprint of the different 1956 volume; ch. 19 of the 1966 work is 10.4324/9781315104645-19.
